title: The switched bride (Genesis 29:21–30)
hook: the trickster is tricked, and wakes to find Leah instead of Rachel

segments.voice: Last week ended with seven years like a few days, for the love Jacob had for Rachel. Your line was love shortens the time. What did you do for love, not the clock? A new week. Day fifty-seven.

Seven years are up. Jacob goes to Laban: give me my wife, my time is done. Laban throws a great wedding feast and invites every man in the place. There's food, there's wine, there's music. And that night, in the dark, Laban brings his daughter to Jacob's tent. The bride is veiled. The tent is dark. And in the old JPS translation, the next verse lands like a slap: "And it came to pass in the morning that, behold, it was Leah." Not Rachel. Her older sister. Picture Jacob waking up, turning over, and seeing the wrong face. After seven years of work. After all that love. Today: the trickster, tricked.
screen: `SEVEN YEARS ARE UP.` → `A FEAST, A VEIL, A DARK TENT.` → `BEHOLD, IT WAS LEAH.`

segments.voice: Jacob storms to Laban: "What is this thou hast done unto me? did not I serve with thee for Rachel? wherefore then hast thou beguiled me?" And Laban answers, calm as anything: "It is not so done in our place, to give the younger before the first-born." Listen to that sentence. The younger before the firstborn. That is exactly what Jacob did to Esau. In a dark tent, with a blind father, Jacob, the younger, put himself in place of the firstborn. Now, in a dark tent, the firstborn is put in place of the younger, and Jacob can't see. And there's a word that ties the two stories together. When Jacob accuses Laban, he says, why have you beguiled me? The Hebrew is from the root of mirmah, deceit. It's the same word Isaac used to Esau: "Thy brother came with guile, and hath taken away thy blessing." The Torah doesn't have to say it's payback. It just uses the same word. A midrash imagines the morning after. Jacob says to Leah: all night I called you Rachel, and you answered. And Leah says: your father called you Esau, and you answered. The rabbis had a name for this pattern: measure for measure. What you do has a way of coming back around. But notice Leah too, standing in the middle of two men's deals, married to someone who wanted her sister. Laban lets Jacob finish the wedding week, then gives him Rachel as well, for another seven years of work. Jacob now has two wives, sisters, and a house built on a trick. We'll hear Leah's side tomorrow.
screen: `WHEREFORE HAST THOU BEGUILED ME?` · `THE YOUNGER BEFORE THE FIRSTBORN.` · `MIRMAH — THE SAME WORD, DECEIT.` · `MEASURE FOR MEASURE.` · then, large: `BEHOLD, IT WAS LEAH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Settle, and breathe. Think of a time something you did came back to you. A shortcut that later cost you. A sharp word that returned in someone else's mouth. Or a kindness that came back, years later, from someone unexpected. It works both ways. Stay with one example. Don't judge it. Just notice the shape of it: out, and back again. If you pray, you can ask to see your own part clearly. The bell holds the time.
The switched bride. Jacob, who took his brother's place in the dark, wakes up to find Leah in the place of Rachel.
Your line: it comes back around. Today, notice one moment when something you did comes back to you, and see what it teaches. Day fifty-seven.

howItsDone: Jews read the switched bride in the Torah portion Vayetze; many trace the custom of the groom lowering the bride's veil himself at the bedeken, so he can see her face, to this story.

fork.setup: you're Jacob. you wake up after your wedding night, and it's Leah, not Rachel. what does Laban tell you?
options: "it is not so done in our place, to give the younger before the first-born."
fork.reveal: the younger before the firstborn: exactly what Jacob did to Esau. the trickster is tricked, measure for measure.

original.note: Hebrew: deceit, guile. the root links Jacob's trick on Esau to Laban's trick on Jacob.

trapdoor: what you thought: a mean father-in-law played a trick.
what it means: the younger son who took the firstborn's place in the dark is given the firstborn daughter in the dark.
what a scholar hears: the root r-m-h in 27:35 (mirmah) and 29:25 (rimmitani), and Genesis Rabbah 70:19's 'your father called you Esau, and you answered'.

notes: Confirm JPS 1917 wording of Genesis 29:25 (both phrases), 29:26 and 27:35.
Midrash of Leah's reply ('your father called you Esau and you answered'): Genesis Rabbah 70:19. Confirm the reference.
Root r-m-h shared by mirmah (27:35) and rimmitani (29:25): confirm.
'Measure for measure' (middah keneged middah) as a rabbinic principle: Mishnah Sotah 1:7. Not cited in the voice; consider adding to sources.
